title: Aluminium Body Repair — Why Your Range Rover or Jaguar Needs a Specialist
excerpt: Modern Range Rovers and Jaguars are built in aluminium, and aluminium does not bend, weld or forgive the way steel does. Here is what a correct repair involves — and what to ask before your car goes in.
body:
If you drive a current Range Rover, Range Rover Sport, Velar, Discovery or almost any Jaguar built in the last decade, the body under the paint is not steel. It is aluminium — and that single fact changes how the car must be repaired after a collision. Aluminium does not bend, weld or forgive the way steel does, which is why the same dent that a general panel shop would pull and fill on a steel car needs a very different approach on yours.

Why Jaguar Land Rover Build in Aluminium

Jaguar has built aluminium-bodied cars since the 2003 XJ, and from the 2013 model year every full-size Range Rover has been built around an all-aluminium body structure. The reason is weight. The aluminium Range Rover was around 400 kilograms lighter than the steel one it replaced, which pays off in handling, braking, fuel economy and emissions. The trade-off is that aluminium is a far more demanding material to repair.

How Aluminium Behaves Differently

Steel has a memory. Push a steel panel out of shape and it can usually be worked back with heat, a hammer and a dolly, and the metal settles. Aluminium has no such memory. It work-hardens as it is moved, so a panel that is pushed and pulled repeatedly becomes brittle and cracks rather than returning to shape. Heat is just as unforgiving: the alloys used in these bodies are heat-treated for strength, and warming them beyond a few hundred degrees quietly destroys that strength without any visible sign. A repair that looks perfect can leave a panel or a structural section far weaker than it was designed to be.

Rivets and Adhesive, Not Welding

Because of this, an aluminium body is not welded together in the way a steel one is. The factory joins panels and structural sections with self-piercing rivets and structural adhesive, and a correct repair does the same. Damaged sections are cut out at points the manufacturer specifies and new sections are riveted and bonded in, using the exact rivet types, adhesive and cure process the factory used. There is no pulling a crushed rail back into line. The repair has to reproduce the original structure, because the way the body absorbs energy in a crash depends on it.

The Damage You Cannot See

Aluminium can also hide its injuries. A rail or a suspension mounting point can be displaced by a few millimetres with no crease, no crack and nothing to see once the bumper is refitted. The only way to know is to measure the body against the manufacturer's data on a jig or a three-dimensional measuring system before any repair is planned. On an aluminium vehicle this step is not optional — it is where the repair actually starts.

Why the Workshop Itself Matters

There is one more requirement that most owners never think about. Steel dust is the enemy of aluminium. If steel particles from grinding or sanding settle on bare aluminium, the two metals set up a galvanic reaction and the aluminium corrodes from that point. For this reason aluminium repair has to be carried out in a dedicated bay, physically separated from steel work, with its own dust extraction and its own set of tools that never touch steel. A shop that repairs both materials on the same floor with the same tools is building corrosion into your car.

What to Ask

Before your Range Rover or Jaguar goes in for collision repair, ask three things. Is the workshop authorised by Jaguar Land Rover for structural repair? Does it have a dedicated aluminium bay and the riveting and bonding equipment the factory procedure calls for? And will the body be measured against manufacturer data before and after the repair? If the answer to any of these is no, the car may come back looking right without being right.

Our Commitment

Eurotech Auto Repair Centre is a factory-authorised Jaguar and Land Rover structural repairer in New Zealand. We repair aluminium bodies the way the factory builds them — in a dedicated aluminium bay, to the manufacturer's documented procedure, with genuine sections, the specified rivets and adhesives, and measurement before and after. Your car leaves us with the strength, safety and value it had before the accident.
